sp.speaker: Cario
sp.stage: SCENE: —The Orchestra represents a public square in Athens. In the background is the house of Chremylus. A ragged old blind man enters, followed by Chremylus and his slave Cario.
sp.p: What an unhappy fate, great gods, to be the slave of a fool! A servant may give the best of advice, but if his master does not follow it, the poor slave must inevitably have his share in the disaster; for fortune does not allow him to dispose of his own body, it belongs to his master who has bought it. Alas! 'tis the way of the world. But the god, Apollo,in tragic style whose oracles the Pythian priestess on her golden tripod makes known to us, deserves my censure, for surely he is a physician and a cunning diviner; and yet my master is leaving his temple infected with mere madness and insists on following a blind man. Is this not opposed to all good sense? It is for us, who see clearly, to guide those who don't; whereas he clings to the trail of a blind fellow and compels me to do the same without answering my questions with ever a word.To Chremylus Aye, master, unless you tell me why we are following this unknown fellow, I will not be silent, but I will worry and torment you, for you cannot beat me because of my sacred chaplet of laurel.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: No, but if you worry me I will take off your chaplets, and then you will only get a sounder thrashing.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: That's an old song! I am going to leave you no peace till you have told me who this man is; and if I ask it, it's entirely because of my interest in you.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Well, be it so. I will reveal it to you as being the most faithful and the most rascally of all my servants. I honored the gods and did what was right, and yet I was none the less poor and unfortunate.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: I know it but too well.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Others amassed wealth —the sacrilegious, the demagogues, the informers, indeed every sort of rascal.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: I believe you.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Therefore I came to consult the oracle of the god, not on my own account, for my unfortunate life is nearing its end, but for my only son; I wanted to ask Apollo if it was necessary for him to become a thorough knave and renounce his virtuous principles, since that seemed to me to be the only way to succeed in life.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: And with what responding tones did the sacred tripod resound?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: You shall know. The god ordered me in plain terms to follow the first man I should meet upon leaving the temple and to persuade him to accompany me home.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: And who was the first one you met?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: This blind man.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: And you are stupid enough not to understand the meaning of such an answer? Why, the god was advising you thereby, and that in the clearest possible way, to bring up your son according to the fashion of your country.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: What makes you think that?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Is it not evident to the blind, that nowadays to do nothing that is right is the best way to get on?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: No, that is not the meaning of the oracle; there must be another that is nobler. If this blind man would tell us who he is and why and with what object he has led us here, we should no doubt understand what our oracle really does mean.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Come, tell us at once who you are, or I shall give effect to my threat. He menaces him. And quick too, be quick, I say.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: I'll thrash you.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Do you understand who he says he is?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: It's to you and not to me that he replies thus: your mode of questioning him was ill-advised. To Plutus Come, friend, if you care to oblige an honest man, answer me.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: I'll knock you down.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Ah! what a pleasant fellow and what a delightful prophecy the god has given you!

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: By Demeter, you'll have no reason to laugh presently. If you don't speak—

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: I will surely do you an ill turn.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Friends—

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: Take yourselves off and leave me.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: No, we won't.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: This, master, is the best thing to do. I'll undertake to secure him the most frightful death; I will lead him to the verge of a precipice and then leave him there, so that he'll break his neck when he pitches over.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Well then, seize him right away.

div.stage: Cario does so.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: Oh, no! Have mercy!

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Will thou speak then?

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: But if you learn who I am, I know well that you will ill-use me and will not let me go again.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: I call the gods to witness that you have naught to fear if you will only speak.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: Well then, first unhand me.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: There! we set you free.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: Listen then, since I must reveal what I had intended to keep a secret. I am Plutus.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Oh! you wretched rascal! You Plutus all the while, and you never said so!

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: You, Plutus, and in this piteous guise! Oh, Phoebus Apollo! oh, ye gods of heaven and hell! Oh, Zeus! is it really and truly as you say?

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Plutus' very own self?

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: His own very self and none other.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: But tell me, how come you're so squalid?

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: I have just left Patrocles' house, who has not had a bath since his birth.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: But your infirmity; how did that happen? Tell me.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: Zeus inflicted it on me, because of his jealousy of mankind. When I was young, I threatened him that I would only go to the just, the wise, the men of ordered life; to prevent my distinguishing these, he struck me with blindness! so much does he envy the good!

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: And yet, it's only the upright and just who honor him.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: Quite true.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Therefore, if ever you recovered your sight, you would shun the wicked?

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: Undoubtedly.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: You would visit the good?

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: Assuredly. It is a very long time since I saw them.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: That's not astonishing. I, who see clearly, don't see a single one.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: Now let me leave you, for I have told you everything.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: No, certainly not! we shall fasten ourselves on to you faster than ever.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: Did I not tell you, you were going to plague me?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Oh! I adjure you, believe what I say and don't leave me; for you will seek in vain for a more honest man than myself.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: There is only one man more worthy; and that is I.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: All talk like this, but as soon as they secure my favours and grow rich, their wickedness knows no bounds.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: And yet all men are not wicked.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: All. There's no exception.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: You shall pay for that opinion.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Listen to what happiness there is in store for you, if you but stay with us. I have hope; aye, I have good hope with the god's help to deliver you from that blindness, in fact to restore your sight.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: Oh! do nothing of the kind, for I don't wish to recover it.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: What's that you say?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: This fellow hugs his own misery.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: If you were mad enough to cure me, and Zeus heard of it, he would overwhelm me with his anger.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: And is he not doing this now by leaving you to grope your wandering way?

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: I don't know; but I'm horribly afraid of him.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Indeed? Ah! you are the biggest poltroon of all the gods! Why, Zeus with his throne and his lightnings would not be worth an obolus if you recovered your sight, were it but for a few moments.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: Impious man, don't talk like that.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Fear nothing! I will prove to you that you are far more powerful and mightier than he.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: I mightier than he?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Aye, by heaven! To Cario For instance, what is the basis of the power that Zeus wields over the other gods?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Money; he has so much of it.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: And who gives it to him?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: This fellow.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: If sacrifices are offered to him, is not Plutus their cause?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Undoubtedly, for it's wealth that all demand and clamor most loudly for.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Thus it's Plutus who is the fount of all the honors rendered to Zeus, whose worship he can wither up at the root, if it so pleases him.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: And how so?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Not an ox, nor a cake, nor indeed anything at all could be offered, if you did not wish it.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Why? but what means are there to buy anything if you are not there to give the money? Hence if Zeus should cause you any trouble, you will destroy his power without other help.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: So it's because of me that sacrifices are offered to him?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Most assuredly. Whatever is dazzling, beautiful or charming in the eyes of mankind, comes from you. Does not everything depend on wealth?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: I myself was bought for a few coins; if I'm a slave, it's only because I was not rich.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: And what of the Corinthian whores? If a poor man offers them proposals, they do not listen; but if it be a rich one, instantly they turn their arses to him.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: It's the same with the lads; they care not for love, to them money means everything.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: You speak of male whores; yet some of them are honest, and it's not money they ask of their patrons.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: What then?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: A fine horse, a pack of hounds.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Yes, they would blush to ask for money and cleverly disguise their shame.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: It is in you that every art, all human inventions, have had their origin; it is through you that one man sits cutting leather in his shop.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: That another fashions iron or wood.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: That yet another chases the gold he has received from you.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: This one steals clothes, by Zeus, and that one is a housebreaker.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: That one is a clothes-cleaner.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: And the other washes bedding.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: That this one is a tanner.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: And that other sells onions.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: And if the adulterer, caught red-handed, is depilated, it's on account of you.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: Oh! great gods! I knew naught of all this!

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Is it not he who lends the Great King all his pride?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Is it not he who draws the citizens to the Assembly?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: And tell me, is it not you who equip the triremes?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: And who feed our mercenaries at Corinth?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Are not you the cause of Pamphilus' sufferings?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: And of the needle-seller's with Pamphilus?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: It is not because of you that Agyrrhius farts so loudly?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: And that Philepsius rolls off his fables? That troops are sent to succour the Egyptians? And that Lais is kept by Philonides?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: That the tower of Timotheus—

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: To Cario May it fall upon your head! To PlutusIn short, Plutus, it is through you that everything is done; you must realize that you are the sole cause both of good and evil.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: In war, it's the flag under which you serve that victory favours.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: What! I can do so many things by myself and unaided?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: And many others besides; wherefore men are never tired of your gifts. They get weary of all else, —of love ...

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Bread.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Music.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Sweetmeats.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Honors.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Cakes.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Battles.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Figs.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Ambition.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Gruel.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Military advancement.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Lentil soup.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: But of you they never tire. If a man has thirteen talents, he has all the greater ardor to possess sixteen; if that wish is achieved, he will want forty or will complain that he knows not how to make both ends meet.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: All this, I suppose, is very true; there is but one point that makes me feel a bit uneasy.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: And that is?

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: How could I use this power, which you say I have?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Ah! they were quite right who said there's nothing more timorous than Plutus.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: No, no; it was a thief who calumniated me. Having broken into a house, he found everything locked up and could take nothing, so he dubbed my prudence fear.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Don't be disturbed; if you support me zealously, I'll make you more sharp-sighted than Lynceus.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: And how should you be able to do that, you, who are but a mortal?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: I have great hope, after the answer Apollo gave me, shaking his sacred laurels the while.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: Is he in the plot then?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Surely.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: Take care what you say.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Never fear, friend; for, be well assured, that if it has to cost me my life, I will carry out what I have in my head.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: And I will help you, if you permit it.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: We shall have many other helpers as well —all the worthy folk who are wanting for bread.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: Ah! they'll prove sorry helpers.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: No, not so, once they've grown rich. But you, Cario, run quick ...

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Where?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: ... to call my comrades, the other husbandmen (you'll probably find the poor fellows toiling away in the fields), that each of them may come here to take his share of the gifts of Plutus.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: I'm off. But let someone come from the house to take this morsel of meat.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: I'll see to that; you run your hardest. As for you, Plutus, the most excellent of all the gods, come in here with me; this is the house you must fill with riches to-day, by fair means or foul.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: I don't at all like going into other folks' houses in this manner; I have never got any good from it. If I got inside a miser's house, straightway he would bury me deep underground; if some honest fellow among his friends came to ask him for the smallest coin, he would deny ever having seen me. Then if I went to a fool's house, he would sacrifice in dicing and wenching, and very soon I should be completely stripped and pitched out of doors.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: That's because you have never met a man who knew how to avoid the two extremes; moderation is the strong point in my character. I love saving as much as anybody, and I know how to spend, when it's needed. But let us go in; I want to make you known to my wife and to my only son, whom I love most of all after yourself.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: I'm quite sure of that.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Why should I hide the truth from you?

div.stage: They enter Chremylus' house.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.stage: To the Chorus, which has followed him in
sp.p: Come, you active workers, who, like my master, eat nothing but garlic and the poorest food, you who are his friends and his neighbors, hasten your steps, hurry yourselves; there's not a moment to lose; this is the critical hour, when your presence and your support are needed by him.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Why, don't you see we are speeding as fast as men can, who are already enfeebled by age? But do you deem it fitting to make us run like this before ever telling us why your master has called us?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: I've grown hoarse with the telling, but you won't listen. My master is going to drag you all out of the stupid, sapless life you are leading and ensure you one full of all delights.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: And how is he going to manage that?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: My poor friends, he has brought with him a disgusting old fellow, all bent and wrinkled, with a most pitiful appearance, bald and toothless; upon my word, I even believe he is circumcised like some vile barbarian.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: This news is worth its weight in gold! What are you saying? Repeat it to me; no doubt it means he is bringing back a heap of wealth.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: No, but a heap of all the infirmities attendant on old age.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: If you are tricking us, you shall pay us for it. Beware of our sticks!

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Do you deem me so brazen as all that, and my words mere lies?

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: What serious airs the rascal puts on! Look! his legs are already shrieking, “oh! oh!” They are asking for the shackles and wedges.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: It's in the tomb that it's your lot to judge. Why don't you go there? Charon has given you your ticket.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Plague take you! you cursed rascal, who rail at us and have not even the heart to tell us why your master has made us come. We were pressed for time and tired out, yet we came with all haste, and in our hurry we have passed by lots of wild onions without even gathering them.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: I will no longer conceal the truth from you. Friends, it's Plutus whom my master brings, Plutus, who will give you riches.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: What! we shall really all become rich?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Aye, certainly; you will then be Midases, provided you grow ass's ears.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: What joy, what happiness! If what you tell me is true, I long to dance with delight.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: And I too, threttanelo! I want to imitate the Cyclops and lead your troop by stamping like this. Do you, my dear little ones, cry, aye, cry again and bleat forth the plaintive song of the sheep and of the stinking goats; follow me like lascivious goats with their tools out.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: As for us, threttanelo! we will seek you, dear Cyclops, bleating, and if we find you with your wallet full of fresh herbs, all disgusting in your filth, sodden with wine and sleeping in the midst of your sheep, we will seize a great flaming stake and burn out your eye.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: I will copy that Circe of Corinth, whose potent philtres compelled the companions of Philonides like swine to swallow balls of dung, which she herself had kneaded with her hands; and do you too grunt with joy and follow your mother, my little pigs.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Oh! Circe with the potent philtres, who besmear your companions so filthily, what pleasure I shall have in imitating the son of Laertes! I will hang you up by your balls, I will rub your nose with dung like a goat, and like Aristyllus you shall say through your half-opened lips, “Follow your mother, my little pigs.”

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Enough of tomfoolery, assume a grave demeanor; unknown to my master I am going to take bread and meat; and when I have fed well, I shall resume my work.
sp.stage: Interlude of dancing by the Chorus.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: To say, “Hail! my dear neighbors!” is an old form of greeting and well worn with use; so therefore I embrace you, because you have not crept like tortoises, but have come rushing here in all haste. Now help me to watch carefully and closely over the god.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Be at ease. You shall see with what martial zeal I will guard him. What! we jostle each other at the Assembly for three obols, and am I going to let Plutus in person be stolen from me?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: But I see Blepsidemus; by his bearing and his haste I can readily see he knows or suspects something.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: What has happened then? Whence, how has Chremylus suddenly grown rich? I don't believe a word of it. Nevertheless, nothing but his sudden fortune was being talked about in the barber-shops. But I am above all surprised that his good fortune has not made him forget his friends; that is not the usual way!

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: By the gods, Blepsidemus, I will hide nothing from you. To-day things are better than yesterday; let us share, for are you not my friend?

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Have you really grown rich as they say?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: I shall be soon, if the god agrees to it. But there is still some risk to run.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: What risk?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Well ...

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Tell me, quick!

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: If we succeed, we are happy for ever, but if we fail, it is all over with us.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: It's a bad business, and one that doesn't please me! To grow rich all at once and yet to be fearful! ah! I suspect something that's little good.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: No doubt you have just stolen some gold and silver from some temple and are repenting.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Nay! heaven preserve me from that!

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: A truce to idle phrases! the thing is only too apparent, my friend.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Don't suspect such a thing of me.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Alas! then there is no honest man! not one, that can resist the attraction of gold!

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: By Demeter, you have no common sense.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: How he has changed!

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: But, good gods, you are mad, my dear fellow!

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: His very look is distraught; he has done some crime!

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Ah! I know the tune you are playing now; you think I have stolen, and want your share.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: My share of what, pray?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: You are beside the mark; the thing is quite otherwise.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Perhaps it's not a theft, but some piece of knavery!

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: You are insane!

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: What? You have done no man an injury?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: No! assuredly not!

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: But, great gods, what am I to think? You won't tell me the truth.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: You accuse me without really knowing anything.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Listen, friend, no doubt the matter can yet be hushed up, before it gets noised abroad, at trifling expense; I will buy the orators' silence.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Aye, you will lay out three minae and, as my friend, you will reckon twelve against me.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: I know someone who will come and seat himself at the foot of the tribunal, holding a supplicant's bough in his hand and surrounded by his wife and children, for all the world like the Heraclidae of Pamphilus.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Not at all, poor fool! But, thanks to me, worthy folk alone shall be rich henceforth.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: What are you saying? Have you then stolen so much as all that?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Oh! your insults will be the death of me.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: You're the one who is courting death.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Not so, you wretch, since I have Plutus.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: You have Plutus? Which one?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: The god himself.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: And where is he?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: There.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Where?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Indoors.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Indoors?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Aye, certainly.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Get you gone! Plutus in your house?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Yes, by the gods!

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Are you telling the truth?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: I am.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Swear it by Hestia.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: I swear it by Poseidon.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: The god of the sea?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Yes, and by all the other Poseidons, if such there be.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: And you don't send him to us, to your friends?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: We've not got to that point yet.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: What do you say? Is there no chance of sharing?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Why, no. We must first ...

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Do what?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: ... restore him his sight.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Restore whom his sight? Speak!

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Plutus. It must be done, no matter how.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Is he then really blind?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Yes, undoubtedly.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: I am no longer surprised he never came to me.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: If it please the gods, he'll come there now.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Must we not go and seek a physician?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Seek physicians at Athens? Nay! there's no art where there's no fee.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.stage: running his eyes over the audience
sp.p: Let's look carefully.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: There is not one.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: It's a positive fact; I don't know of one.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: But I have thought the matter well over, and the best thing is to make Plutus lie in the Temple of Asclepius.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Unquestionably that's the very best thing. Hurry and lead him away to the temple.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: I am going there.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Then hurry up.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: That's just what I am doing.

div.stage: They are just leaving when Poverty comes running in; she is a picture of squalor and the two men recoil in horror.

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: Unwise, perverse, unholy men! What are you daring to do, you pitiful, wretched mortals? Whither are you flying? Stop! I command it!

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Oh! great gods!

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: My arm shall destroy you, you infamous beings! Such an attempt is not to be borne; neither man nor god has ever dared the like. You shall die!

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: And who are you? Oh! what a ghastly pallor!

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Perhaps it's some Erinys, some Fury, from the theater; there's a kind of wild tragic look in her eyes.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: But she has no torch.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Let's knock her down!

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: Who do you think I am?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Some wine-shop keeper or egg-woman. Otherwise you would not have shrieked so loud at us, who have done nothing to you.

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: Indeed? And have you not done me the most deadly injury by seeking to banish me from every country?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Why, have you not got the Barathrum left? But who are you? Answer me quickly!

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: I am one that will punish you this very day for having wanted to make me disappear from here.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Might it be the tavern-keeper in my neighborhood, who is always cheating me in measure?

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: I am Poverty, who have lived with you for so many years.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Oh! great Apollo! oh, ye gods! whither shall I fly?

div.stage: He starts to run away.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Here! what are you doing! You coward! Are you going to leave me here?

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Not I.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Stop then! Are two men to run away from one woman?

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: But, you wretch, it's Poverty, the most fearful monster that ever drew breath.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Stay where you are, I beg of you.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: No! no! a thousand times, no!

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Could we do anything worse than leave the god in the lurch and fly before this woman without so much as ever offering to fight?

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: But what weapons have we? Are we in a condition to show fight? Where is the breastplate, the buckler, that this wretch has not pawned?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Be at ease. Plutus will readily triumph over her threats unaided.

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: Dare you reply, you scoundrels, you who are caught red-handed at the most horrible crime?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: As for you, you cursed jade, you pursue me with your abuse, though I have never done you the slightest harm.

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: Do you think it is doing me no harm to restore Plutus to the use of his eyes?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Is this doing you harm, that we shower blessings on all men?

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: And what do you think will ensure their happiness?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Ah! first of all we shall drive you out of Greece.

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: Drive me out? Could you do mankind a greater harm?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Yes —if I gave up my intention to deliver them from you.

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: Well, let us discuss this point first. I propose to show that I am the sole cause of all your blessings, and that your safety depends on me alone. If I don't succeed, then do what you like to me.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: How dare you talk like this, you impudent hussy?

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: Agree to hear me and I think it will be very easy for me to prove that you are entirely on the wrong road, when you want to make the just men wealthy.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Oh! cudgel and rope's end, come to my help!

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: Why such wrath and these shouts, before you hear my arguments?

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: But who could listen to such words without exclaiming?

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: Any man of sense.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: But if you lose your case, what punishment will you submit to?

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: Choose what you will.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: That's all right.

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: You shall suffer the same if you are beaten!

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Do you think twenty deaths a sufficiently large stake?

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Good enough for her, but for us two would suffice.

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: You won't escape, for is there indeed a single valid argument to oppose me with?

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: To beat her in this debate, you must call upon all your wits. Make no allowances and show no weakness!

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: It is right that the good should be happy, that the wicked and the impious, on the other hand, should be miserable; that is a truth, I believe, which no one will gainsay. To realize this condition of things is a proposal as great as it is noble and useful in every respect, and we have found a means of attaining the object of our wishes. If Plutus recovers his sight and ceases from wandering about unseeing and at random, he will go to seek the just men and never leave them again; he will shun the perverse and ungodly; so, thanks to him, all men will become honest, rich and pious. Can anything better be conceived for the public weal?

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Of a certainty, no! I bear witness to that. It is not even necessary she should reply.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Does it not seem that everything is extravagance in the world, or rather madness, when you watch the way things go? A crowd of rogues enjoy blessings they have won by sheer injustice, while more honest folks are miserable, die of hunger, and spend their whole lives with you. Now, if Plutus became clear-sighted again and drove out Poverty, it would be the greatest blessing possible for the human race.

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: Here are two old men, whose brains are easy to confuse, who assist each other to talk rubbish and drivel to their hearts' content. But if your wishes were realized, your profit would be great! Let Plutus recover his sight and divide his favours out equally to all, and none will ply either trade or art any longer; all toil would be done away with. Who would wish to hammer iron, build ships, sew, turn, cut up leather, bake bricks, bleach linen, tan hides, or break up the soil of the earth with the plough and garner the gifts of Demeter, if he could live in idleness and free from all this work?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: What nonsense all this is! All these trades which you just mention will be plied by our slaves.

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: Your slaves! And by what means will these slaves be got?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: We will buy them.

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: But first say, who will sell them, if everyone is rich?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Some greedy dealer from Thessaly —the land which supplies so many.

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: But if your system is applied, there won't be a single slave-dealer left. What rich man would risk his life to devote himself to this traffic? You will have to toil, to dig and submit yourself to all kinds of hard labour; so that your life would be more wretched even than it is now.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: May this prediction fall upon yourself!

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: You will not be able to sleep in a bed, for no more will ever be manufactured; nor no carpets, for who would weave them, if he had gold? When you bring a young bride to your dwelling, you will have no essences wherewith to perfume her, nor rich embroidered cloaks dyed with dazzling colors in which to clothe her. And yet what is the use of being rich, if you are to be deprived of all these enjoyments? On the other hand, you have all that you need in abundance, thanks to me; to the artisan I am like a severe mistress, who forces him by need and poverty to seek the means of earning his livelihood.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: And what good thing can you give us, unless it be burns in the bath, and swarms of brats and old women who cry with hunger, and clouds uncountable of lice, gnats and flies, which hover about the wretch's head, trouble him, awake him and say, “You will be hungry, but get up!” Besides, to possess a rag in place of a mantle, a pallet of rushes swarming with bugs, that do not let you close your eyes, for a bed; a rotten piece of matting for a coverlet; a big stone for a pillow, on which to lay your head; to eat mallow roots instead of bread, and leaves of withered radish instead of cake; to have nothing but the cover of a broken jug for a stool, the stave of a cask, and broken at that, for a kneading-trough, that is the life you make for us! Are these the mighty benefits with which you pretend to load mankind?

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: It's not my life that you describe; you are attacking the existence beggars lead.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Is Beggary not Poverty's sister?

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: Thrasybulus and Dionysius are one and the same according to you. No, my life is not like that and never will be. The beggar, whom you have depicted to us, never possesses anything. The poor man lives thriftily and attentive to his work; he has not got too much, but he does not lack what he really needs.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Oh! what a happy life, by Demeter! to live sparingly, to toil incessantly and not to leave enough to pay for a tomb!

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: That's it! Jest, jeer, and never talk seriously! But what you don't know is this, that men with me are worth more, both in mind and body, than with Plutus. With him they are gouty, big-bellied, heavy of limb and scandalously stout; with me they are thin, wasp-waisted, and terrible to the foe.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: No doubt it's by starving them that you give them that waspish waist.

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: As for behavior, I will prove to you that modesty dwells with me and insolence with Plutus.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Oh! the sweet modesty of stealing and burglary.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: †By Zeus, how is it not modesty if you have to go unnoticed?

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: Look at the orators in our republics; as long as they are poor, both state and people can only praise their uprightness; but once they are fattened on the public funds, they conceive a hatred for justice, plan intrigues against the people and attack the democracy.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: That is absolutely true, although your tongue is very vile. But it matters not, so don't put on those triumphant airs; you shall not be punished any the less for having tried to persuade me that poverty is worth more than wealth.

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: Not being able to refute my arguments, you chatter at random and exert yourself to no purpose.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Then tell me this, why does all mankind flee from you?

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: Because I make them better. Children do the very same; they flee from the wise counsels of their fathers. So difficult is it to see one's true interest.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Will you say that Zeus cannot discern what is best? Well, he takes Plutus to himself ...

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: ... and banishes Poverty to the earth.

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: Ah me! how purblind you are, you old fellows of the days of Cronus! Why, Zeus is poor, and I will clearly prove it to you. In the Olympic games, which he founded, and to which he convokes the whole of Greece every four years, why does he only crown the victorious athletes with wild olive? If he were rich he would give them gold.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: That's the way he shows that he clings to his wealth; he is sparing with it, won't part with any portion of it, only bestows baubles on the victors and keeps his money for himself.

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: But wealth coupled to such sordid greed is yet more shameful than poverty.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: May Zeus destroy you, both you and your chaplet of wild olive!

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: Thus you dare to maintain that Poverty is not the fount of all blessings!

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Ask Hecate whether it is better to be rich or starving; she will tell you that the rich send her a meal every month and that the poor make it disappear before it is even served.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: But go and hang yourself and don't breathe another syllable. I will not be convinced against my will.

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: “Oh! citizens of Argos! do you hear what he says?”

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Invoke Pauson, your boon companion, rather.

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: Alas! what is to become of me?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Get you gone, be off quick and a pleasant journey to you.

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: But where shall I go?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: To gaol; but hurry up, let us put an end to this.

sp.speaker: Poverty
sp.p: One day you will recall me.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Then you can return; but disappear for the present. I prefer to be rich; you are free to knock your head against the walls in your rage.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: And I too welcome wealth. I want, when I leave the bath all perfumed with essences, to feast bravely with my wife and children and to fart in the faces of toilers and Poverty.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: So that hussy has gone at last! But let us make haste to put Plutus to bed in the Temple of Asclepius.

sp.speaker: Blepsidemus
sp.p: Let us make haste; else some bothering fellow may again come to interrupt us.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Cario, bring the coverlets and all that I have got ready from the house; let us conduct the god to the temple, taking care to observe all the proper rites.

div.stage: Cario comes out of the house with a bundle under one arm and leading Plutus with the other. Chremylus and Blepsidemus join him and all four of them depart.
Interlude of dancing by the Chorus.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Oh! you old fellows, who used to dip out the broth served to the poor at the festival of Theseus with little pieces of bread hollowed like a spoon, how worthy of envy is your fate! How happy you are, both you and all just men!

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: My good fellow, what has happened to your friends? You seem the bearer of good tidings.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: What joy for my master and even more for Plutus! The god has regained his sight; his eyes sparkle with the greatest brilliancy, thanks to the benevolent care of Asclepius.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Oh! what transports of joy! oh! what shouts of gladness!

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Aye! one is compelled to rejoice, whether one wants to or not.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: I will sing to the honor of Asclepius, the son of illustrious Zeus, with a resounding voice; he is the beneficent star which men adore.

sp.speaker: Chremylus' Wife
sp.p: What mean these shouts? Is there good news? With what impatience have I been waiting in the house, and for so long too!

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Quick! quick, some wine, mistress. And drink some yourself,Aside it's much to your taste. I bring you all blessings in a lump.

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: Where are they?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: In my words, as you are going to see.

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: Have done with trifling! come, speak.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Listen, I am going to tell you everything from the feet to the head.

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: Oh! don't throw anything at my head.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Not even the happiness that has come to you?

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: No, no, nothing ... to annoy me.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Having arrived near to the temple with our patient, then so unfortunate, but now at the apex of happiness, of blessedness, we first led him down to the sea to purify him.

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: Ah! what a singular pleasure for an old man to bathe in the cold sea-water!

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.stage: in the manner of the tragic messenger
sp.p: Then we repaired to the temple of the god. Once the wafers and the various offerings had been consecrated upon the altar, and the cake of wheaten-meal had been handed over to the devouring Hephaestus, we made Plutus lie on a couch according to the rite, and each of us prepared himself a bed of leaves.

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: Had any other folk come to beseech the deity?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Yes. Firstly, Neoclides, who is blind, but steals much better than those who see clearly; then many others attacked by complaints of all kinds. The lights were put out and the priest enjoined us to sleep, especially recommending us to keep silent should we hear any noise. There we were all lying down quite quietly. I could not sleep; I was thinking of a certain stew-pan full of pap placed close to an old woman and just behind her head. I had a furious longing to slip towards that side. But just as I was lifting my head, I noticed the priest, who was sweeping off both the cakes and the figs on the sacred table; then he made the round of the altars and sanctified the cakes that remained, by stowing them away in a bag. I therefore resolved to follow such a pious example and made straight for the pap.

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: You rogue! and had you no fear of the god?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Aye, indeed! I feared that the god with his crown on his head might have been near the stew-pan before me. I said to myself, “Like priest, like god.” On hearing the noise I made, the old woman put out her hand, but I hissed and bit it, just as a sacred serpent might have done. Quick she drew back her hand, slipped down into the bed with her head beneath the coverlets and never moved again; only she let flee a fart in her fear which stank worse than a weasel. As for myself, I swallowed a goodly portion of the pap and, having made a good feed, went back to bed.

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: And did not the god come?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: He did not tarry; and when he was near us, oh! dear! such a good joke happened. My belly was quite blown up, and I let a thunderous fart!

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: Doubtless the god pulled a wry face?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: No, but Iaso blushed a little and Panacea turned her head away, holding her nose; my farts are not perfume.

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: And what did the god do?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: He paid not the slightest heed.

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: He must then be a pretty coarse kind of god?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: I don't say that, but he's used to tasting stools.

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: Impudent knave, go on with you!

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Then I hid myself in my bed all a-tremble. Asclepius did the round of the patients and examined them all with great attention; then a slave placed beside him a stone mortar, a pestle and a little box.

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: Of stone?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: No, not of stone.

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: But how could you see all this, you arch-rascal, when you say you were hiding all the time?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Why, great gods, through my cloak, for it's not without holes! He first prepared an ointment for Neoclides; he threw three heads of Tenian garlic into the mortar, pounded them with an admixture of fig-tree sap and lentisk, moistened the whole with Sphettian vinegar, and, turning back the patient's eyelids, applied his salve to the interior of the eyes, so that the pain might be more excruciating. Neoclides shrieked, howled, sprang towards the foot of his bed and wanted to bolt, but the god laughed and said to him, “Keep where you are with your salve; by doing this you will not go and perjure yourself before the Assembly.”

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: What a wise god and what a friend to our city!

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Thereupon he came and seated himself at the head of Plutus' bed, took a perfectly clean rag and wiped his eyelids; Panacea covered his head and face with a purple cloth, while the god whistled, and two enormous snakes came rushing from the sanctuary.

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: Great gods!

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: They slipped gently beneath the purple cloth and, as far as I could judge, licked the patient's eyelids; for, in less time than even you need, mistress, to drain down ten beakers of wine, Plutus rose up; he could see. I clapped my hands with joy and awoke my master, and the god immediately disappeared with the serpents into the sanctuary. As for those who were lying near Plutus, you can imagine that they embraced him tenderly. Dawn broke and not one of them had closed an eye. As for myself, I did not cease thanking the god who had so quickly restored to Plutus his sight and had made Neoclides blinder than ever.

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: Oh! thou great Asclepius! How mighty is thy power! To Cario But tell me, where is Plutus now?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: He is approaching, escorted by an immense crowd. The rich, whose wealth is ill-gotten, are knitting their brows and shooting at him looks of fierce hate, while the just folk, who led a wretched existence, embrace him and grasp his hand in the transport of their joy; they follow in his wake, their heads wreathed with garlands, laughing and blessing their deliverer; the old men make the earth resound as they walk together keeping time. Come, all of you, all, down to the very least, dance, leap and form yourselves into a chorus; no longer do you risk being told, when you go home. “There is no meal in the bag.”

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: And I, by Hecate! I will string you a garland of cakes for the good tidings you have brought me.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Hurry, make haste then; our friends are close at hand.

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: I will go indoors to fetch some gifts of welcome, to celebrate these eyes that have just been opened.

div.stage: She goes back into the house.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Meantime I am going forth to meet them.

div.stage: Exit
Interlude of dancing by the Chorus.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: I adore thee, oh! thou divine sun, and thee I greet, thou city, the beloved of Pallas; be welcome, thou land of Cecrops, which hast received me. Alas! what manner of men I associated with! I blush to think of it. While, on the other hand, I shunned those who deserved my friendship; I knew neither the vices of the ones nor the virtues of the others. A two-fold mistake, and in both cases equally fatal! Ah! what a misfortune was mine! But I want to change everything; and in the future I mean to prove to mankind that, if I gave to the wicked, it was against my will.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Get you gone! Oh! what a lot of friends spring into being when you are fortunate! They dig me with their elbows and bruise my shins to prove their affection. Each one wants to greet me. What a crowd of old fellows thronged round me on the market-place!

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: Oh! thou, who art dearest of all to me, and thou too, be welcome! Allow me, Plutus, to shower these gifts of welcome over you in due accord with custom.

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: No. This is the first house I enter after having regained my sight; I shall take nothing from it, for it is my place rather to give.

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: Do you refuse these gifts?

sp.speaker: Plutus
sp.p: I will accept them at your fireside, as custom requires. Besides, we shall thus avoid a ridiculous scene; it is not meet that the poet should throw dried figs and dainties to the spectators; it is a vulgar trick to make them laugh.

sp.speaker: Wife
sp.p: You are right. Look! yonder's Dexinicus, who was already getting to his feet to catch the figs as they flew past him.

div.stage: Interlude of dancing by the Chorus.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: How pleasant it is, friends, to live well, especially when it costs nothing! What a deluge of blessings flood our household, and that too without our having wronged a single soul! [Ah! what a delightful thing is wealth!] The bin is full of white flour and the wine-jars run over with fragnant liquor; all the chests are crammed with gold and silver, it is a sight to see; the tank is full of oil, the phials with perfumes, and the garret with dried figs. Vinegar flasks, plates, stew-pots and all the platters are of brass; our rotten old wooden trenchers for the fish have to-day become dishes of silver; even the thunder-mug is of ivory. We others, the slaves, we play at odd and even with gold pieces, and carry luxury so far that we no longer wipe our arses with stones, but use garlic stalks instead. My master, at this moment, is crowned with flowers and sacrificing a pig, a goat and a ram; it's the smoke that has driven me out, for I could no longer endure it, it hurt my eyes so.

div.stage: A Just Man enters, followed by a small slave-lad who carries a threadbare cloak and a pair of badly worn sandals.

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: Come, my child, come with me. Let us go and find the god.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Who's this?

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: A man who was once wretched, but now is happy.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: A just man then?

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Well! what do you want?

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: I come to thank the god for all the blessings he has showered on me. My father had left me a fairly decent fortune, and I helped those of my friends who were in want; it was, to my thinking, the most useful thing I could do with my fortune.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: And you were quickly ruined?

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: Quite.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: And since then you have been living in misery?

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: Quite; I thought I could count, in case of need, upon the friends whose property I had helped, but they turned their backs upon me and pretended not to see me.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: They laughed at you, that's obvious.

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: Quite. With my empty coffers, I had no more friends.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: But that's no longer so.

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: My lot has changed, and so I come to the god to make him the acts of gratitude that are his due.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: But why are you bringing this old cloak, which your slave is carrying? Tell me.

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: I wish to dedicate it to the god.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Were you initiated into the Great Mysteries in that cloak?

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: No, but I shivered in it for thirteen years.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: And this footwear?

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: These also are my winter companions.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: And you wish to dedicate them too?

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: Certainly.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Fine presents to offer to the god!

div.stage: An Informer enters, followed by a witness.

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: Alas! alas! I am a lost man. Ah! thrice, four, five, twelve times, or rather ten thousand times unhappy fate! Why, why must fortune deal me such rough blows?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Oh, Apollo, my tutelary! oh! ye favourable gods! what has overtaken this man?

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: Ah! am I not deserving of pity? I have lost everything; this cursed god has stripped me bare. Ah! if there be justice in heaven, he shall be struck blind again.

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: I think I know what's the matter. If this man is unfortunate, it's because he's of little account and small honesty; and indeed he looks it too.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Then, by Zeus! his plight is but just.

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: He promised that if he recovered his sight, he would enrich us all unaided; whereas he has ruined more than one.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: But whom has he thus ill-used?

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: Me.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: You were doubtless a villainous thief then.

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: No, it is rather you yourselves who were such wretches; I am certain you have got my money.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Ha! by Demeter! an informer! What impudence! He's ravenously hungry, that's certain.

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: You shall follow me this very instant to the market-place, where the torture of the wheel shall force the confession of your misdeeds from you.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Watch out, now!

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: By Zeus the Deliverer, what gratitude all Greeks owe to Plutus, if he destroys these vile informers!

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: You are laughing at me. Well, then I denounce you as their accomplice. Where did you steal that new cloak from? Yesterday I saw you with one utterly worn out.

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: I fear you not, thanks to this ring, for which I paid Eudemus a drachma.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: †Ah! there's no ring to preserve you from the informer's bite.†

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: The insolent wretches! But, my fine jokers, you have not told me what you are up to here. Nothing good, I'm sure of that.

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: Nothing of any good for you, be sure of that.

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: By Zeus! it's at my expense that you are about to dine.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: You and your witness, I hope you both burst with an empty belly.

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: You deny it? I reckon, you villains, that there is much salt fish and roast meat in this house.He sniffs elaborately.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Can you smell anything, rascal?

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: The cold, perhaps, with that ragged cloak around you.

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: Can such outrages be borne, oh, Zeus! Ye gods! how cruel it is to see me treated thus, when I am such an honest fellow and such a good citizen!

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: You an honest man! you a good citizen!

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: A better one than any.

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: Ah! well then, answer my questions.

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: Concerning what?

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: Are you a husbandman?

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: D'ye take me for a fool?

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: A merchant?

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: I assume the title, when it serves me.

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: Do you ply any trade?

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: No, most assuredly not!

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: Then how do you live, if you do nothing?

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: I superintend public and private business.

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: You do? And by what right, pray?

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: Because it pleases me to do so.

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: Like a thief you sneak yourself in where you have no business. You are hated by all and you claim to be an honest man.

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: What, you fool? I have not the right to dedicate myself entirely to my country's service?

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: Is the country served by vile intrigue?

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: It is served by watching that the established law is observed —by allowing no one to violate it.

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: That's the duty of the tribunals; they are established to that end.

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: And who is the prosecutor before the dicasts?

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: Whoever wishes to be.

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: Well then, it is I who choose to be prosecutor; and thus all public affairs fall within my province.

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: I pity Athens for being in such vile clutches. But would you not prefer to live quietly and free from all care and anxiety?

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: To do nothing is to live an animal's life.

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: Thus you will not change your mode of life?

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: No, though they gave me Plutus himself and the silphium of Battus.

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: Come, quick, off with your cloak.

div.stage: The Informer does not move.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Hi! friend! it's you they are speaking to.

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: Off with your shoes.

div.stage: The Informer still remains motionless.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: I say, all this is addressed to you.

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: Very well! let one of you come near me, if he dares.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: I dare.

div.stage: He strips the Informer of his cloak and shoes. The witness runs away.

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: Alas! I am robbed of my clothes in full daylight.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: That's what comes of meddling with other folk's business and living at their expense.

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.stage: Over his shoulder to the departing witness
sp.p: You see what is happening; I call you to witness.

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: Look how the witness whom you brought is taking to his heels.

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: Great gods! I am all alone and they assault me.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Shout away!

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: Oh! woe, woe is me!

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Give me that old ragged cloak, that I may dress out the informer.

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: No, no; I have dedicated it to Plutus.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: And where would your offering be better bestowed than on the shoulders of a rascal and a thief? To Plutus fine, rich cloaks should be given.

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: And what then shall be done with these shoes? Tell me.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: I will nail them to his brow as gifts are nailed to the trunks of the wild olive.

sp.speaker: Informer
sp.p: I'm off, for you are the strongest, I own. But if I find someone to join me, let him be as weak as he will, I will summon this god, who thinks himself so strong, before the court this very day, and denounce him as manifestly guilty of overturning the democracy by his will alone and without the consent of the Senate or the Assembly.

sp.speaker: Just Man
sp.p: Now that you are rigged out from head to foot with my old clothes, hasten to the bath and stand there in the front row to warm yourself better; that's the place I formerly had.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Ah! the bath-man would grab you by the balls and fling you through the door; he would only need to see you to appraise you at your true value. ... But let us go in, friend, that you may address your thanksgivings to the god.

div.stage: Interlude of dancing by the Chorus.
An Old Woman enters, dressed as a young girl and trying to walk in a youthful and alluring manner. She carries a plate of food.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: My dear old men, am I near the house where the new god lives, or have I missed the road?

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: You are at his door, my pretty little maid, who question us so sweetly.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: Then I will summon someone in the house.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: No need. I am here myself. But what brings you here?

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: Ah! a cruel, unjust fate! My dear friend, this god has made life unbearable to me through ceasing to be blind.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: What does this mean? Can you be a female informer?

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: Most certainly not.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Have you drunk up your money then?

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: You are mocking me! No! I am being devoured with a consuming fire.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Then tell me what is consuming you so fiercely.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: Listen! I loved a young man, who was poor, but so handsome, so well-built, so honest! He readily gave way to all I desired and acquitted himself so well! I, for my part, refused him nothing.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: And what did he generally ask of you?

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: Very little; he bore himself towards me with astonishing discretion! perchance twenty drachmae for a cloak or eight for footwear; sometimes he begged me to buy tunics for his sisters or a little mantle for his mother; at times he needed four bushels of corn.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: That's very little, in truth; I admire his modesty.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: And it wasn't as a reward for his complacency that he ever asked me for anything, but as a matter of pure friendship; a cloak I had given would remind him from whom he had got it.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: It was a fellow who loved you madly.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: But it's no longer so, for the faithless wretch has sadly altered! I had sent him this cake with the sweetmeats you see here on this dish and let him know that I would visit him in the evening ...

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Well?

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: He sent me back my presents and added this tart to them, on condition that I never set foot in his house again. Besides, he sent me this message, “Once upon a time the Milesians were brave.”

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: An honest lad, indeed! What do you expect? When poor, he would devour anything; now he is rich, he no longer cares for lentils.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: Formerly he came to me every day.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: To see if you were being buried?

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: No! he longed to hear the sound of my voice.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: And to carry off some present.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: If I was downcast, he would call me his little duck or his little dove in a most tender manner ...

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: And then would ask for the money to buy a pair of sandals.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: When I was at the Mysteries of Eleusis in a carriage, someone made eyes at me; he was so jealous that he beat me the whole of that day.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: That was because he liked to feed alone.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: He told me I had very beautiful hands.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Aye, no doubt, when they handed him twenty drachmae.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: That my whole body breathed a sweet perfume.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Yes, like enough, if you poured him out Thasian wine.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: That my glance was gentle and charming.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: He was no fool. He knew how to drag drachmae from a sex-starved old woman.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: Ah! the god has done very, very wrong, saying he would support the victims of injustice.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Well, what should he do? Speak, and it shall be done.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: Compel him, whom I have loaded with benefits, to repay them in his turn; if not, he does not merit the least of the god's favours.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: And did he not do this every night?

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: He swore he would never leave me, as long as I lived.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Aye, rightly; but he thinks you are no longer alive.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: Ah! friend, I am pining away with grief.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: You are rotting away, it seems to me.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: I have grown so thin, I could slip through a ring.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Yes, if it were as large as the hoop of a sieve.

div.stage: A young man enters, wearing a garland on his head and carrying a torch in his hand.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: But here is the youth, the cause of my complaint; he looks as though he were going to a festival.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Yes, if his chaplet and his torch are any guides.

sp.speaker: Youth
sp.stage: To the Old Woman, with cool politeness
sp.p: Greeting to you.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: What was that he said?

sp.speaker: Youth
sp.p: My ancient old dear, you have grown white very quickly, by heaven!

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: Oh! what an insult!

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: It is a long time, then, since he saw you?

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: A long time? My god! he was with me yesterday.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: It must be, then, that, unlike other people, he sees more clearly when he's drunk.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: No, but I have always known him for an insolent fellow.

sp.speaker: Youth
sp.p: Oh! divine Poseidon! Oh, ye gods of old age! what wrinkles she has on her face!

div.stage: He holds his torch close to her, in order to inspect her more closely.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: Oh! oh! keep your distance with that torch.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: It's just as well; if a single spark were to reach her, she would catch fire like an old olive branch.

sp.speaker: Youth
sp.p: I propose to have a game with you.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: Where, naughty boy?

sp.speaker: Youth
sp.p: Here. Take some nuts in your hand.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: What game is this?

sp.speaker: Youth
sp.p: Let's play at guessing how many ... teeth you have.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Ah! I'll tell you; she's got three, or perhaps four.

sp.speaker: Youth
sp.p: Pay up; you've lost! she has only one single grinder.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: You wretch! you're not in your right senses. Do you insult me thus before this crowd?

sp.speaker: Youth
sp.p: I am washing you thoroughly; that's doing you a service.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: No, no! as she is there, she can still deceive; but if this white-lead is washed off, her wrinkles will come out plainly.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: You are only an old fool!

sp.speaker: Youth
sp.p: Ah! he is playing the gallant, he is playing with your tits, and thinks I do not see it.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: Oh! no, by Aphrodite, don't do that, you naughty jealous fellow.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Oh! most certainly not, by Hecate! Verily and indeed I would need to be mad! But, young man, I cannot forgive you, if you cast off this beautiful child.

sp.speaker: Youth
sp.p: Why, I adore her.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: But nevertheless she accuses you ...

sp.speaker: Youth
sp.p: Accuses me of what?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: ... of having told her insolently, “Once upon a time the Milesians were brave.”

sp.speaker: Youth
sp.p: Oh! I shall not dispute with you about her.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Why not?

sp.speaker: Youth
sp.p: Out of respect for your age; with anyone but you I should not be so easy; come, take the girl and be happy.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: I see, I see; you don't want her any more.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: Nay! this is a thing that cannot be allowed.

sp.speaker: Youth
sp.p: I cannot argue with a woman who has been laid by every one of these thirteen thousand men.

div.stage: He points to the audience.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Yet, since you liked the wine, you should now consume the lees.

sp.speaker: Youth
sp.p: But these lees are quite rancid and fusty.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Pass them through a straining-cloth; they'll clarify.

sp.speaker: Youth
sp.p: But I want to go in with you to offer these chaplets to the god.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: And I too have something to tell him.

sp.speaker: Youth
sp.p: Then I won't enter.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Come, have no fear; she won't harm you.

sp.speaker: Youth
sp.p: That's true; I've been managing the old bark so long.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: Go in; I'll follow after you.

div.stage: They enter the house.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Good gods! that old hag has fastened herself to her youth like a limpet to its rock.

div.stage: He follows them in.
Interlude of dancing by the Chorus.
Hermes enters and begins knocking on the door.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Who is knocking at the door? Halloa! I see no one; it was then by chance it gave forth that plaintive tone.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.stage: To Cario, who is about to close the door
sp.p: Cario! stop!

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Eh! friend, was it you who knocked so loudly? Tell me.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: No, I was going to knock and you forestalled me by opening. Come, call your master quick, then his wife and his children, then his slave and his dog, then yourself and his pig.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: And what's it all about?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: It's about this, rascal! Zeus wants to serve you all with the same sauce and hurl the lot of you into the Barathrum.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Have a care for your tongue, you bearer of ill tidings!To Hermes But why does he want to treat us in that scurvy fashion?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Because you have committed the most dreadful crime. Since Plutus has recovered his sight, there is nothing for us other gods, neither incense, nor laurels, nor cakes, nor victims, nor anything in the world.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: And you will never be offered anything more; you governed us too ill.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: I care nothing at all about the other gods, but it's myself. I tell you I am dying of hunger.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: That's reasoning like a wise fellow.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Formerly, from earliest dawn, I was offered all sorts of good things in the wine-shops, —wine-cakes, honey, dried figs, in short, dishes worthy of Hermes. Now, I lie the livelong day on my back, with my legs in the air, famishing.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: And quite right too, for you often had them punished who treated you so well.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Ah! the lovely cake they used to knead for me on the fourth of the month!

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: You recall it vainly; your regrets are useless!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Ah! the ham I was wont to devour!

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Well then! make use of your legs and hop on one leg upon the wineskin, to while away the time.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Oh! the grilled entrails I used to swallow down!

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Your own have got the colic, I think.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Oh! the delicious tipple, half-wine, half-water!

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Here, take this and be off.

div.stage: He farts.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Would you render service to the friend that loves you?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Willingly, if I can.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Give me some well-baked bread and a big hunk of the victims they are sacrificing in your house.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: That would be stealing.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Do you forget, then, how I used to take care he knew nothing about it when you were stealing something from your master?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Because I used to share it with you, you rogue; some cake or other always came your way.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Which afterwards you ate up all by yourself.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: But then you did not share the blows when I was caught.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Forget past injuries, now you have taken Phyle. Ah! how I should like to live with you! Take pity and receive me.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: You would leave the gods to stop here?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: One is much better off among you.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: What! you would desert! Do you think that is honest?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: “Where I live well, there is my country.”

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: But how could we employ you here?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Place me near the door; I am the watchman god and would shift off the robbers.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Shift off! Ah! but we have no love for shifts.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Entrust me with business dealings.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: But we are rich; why should we keep a haggling Hermes?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Let me intrigue for you.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: No, no, intrigues are forbidden; we believe in good faith.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: I will work for you as a guide.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: But the god sees clearly now, so we no longer want a guide.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Well then, I will preside over the games. Ah! what can you object to in that? Nothing is fitter for Plutus than to give scenic and gymnastic games.

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: How useful it is to have so many names! Here you have found the means of earning your bread. I don't wonder the jurymen so eagerly try to get entered for many tribunals.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: So then, you admit me on these terms?

sp.speaker: Cario
sp.p: Go and wash the entrails of the victims at the well, so that you may show yourself serviceable at once.

div.stage: They both enter the house.
A Priest of Zeus comes hurrying in.

sp.speaker: Priest
sp.p: Can anyone tell me where Chremylus is?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: What would you with him, friend?

sp.speaker: Priest
sp.p: Much ill. Since Plutus has recovered his sight, I am perishing of starvation; I, the priest of Zeus the Deliverer, have nothing to eat!

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: And what is the cause of that, pray?

sp.speaker: Priest
sp.p: No one dreams of offering sacrifices.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Why not?

sp.speaker: Priest
sp.p: Because all men are rich. Ah! when they had nothing, the merchant who escaped from shipwreck, the accused who was acquitted, all immolated victims; another would sacrifice for the success of some wish and the priest joined in at the feast; but now there is not the smallest victim, not one of the faithful in the temple, but thousands who come there to take a crap.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Why don't you take your share of those offerings?

sp.speaker: Priest
sp.p: Hence I think I too am going to say good-bye to Zeus the Deliverer, and stop here myself.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Be at ease, all will go well, if it so please the god. Zeus the Deliverer is here; he came of his own accord.

sp.speaker: Priest
sp.p: Ha! that's good news.

div.stage: He moves toward the door.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Wait a little; we are going to install Plutus presently in the place he formerly occupied behind the Temple of Athena; there he will watch over our treasures for ever. Calling out Let lighted torches be brought to the priest. Take these and walk in solemn procession in front of the god.

sp.speaker: Priest
sp.p: That's magnificent!

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Let Plutus be summoned.

div.stage: Plutus comes out of the house, followed by the Old Woman.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: And I, what am I to do?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Take the pots of vegetables which we are going to offer to the god in honor of his installation and carry them on your head; you just happen luckily to be wearing a beautiful embroidered robe.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: And what about the object of my coming?

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Everything shall be according to your wish. The young man will be with you this evening.

sp.speaker: Old Woman
sp.p: Oh! if you promise me his visit, I will right willingly carry the pots.

div.stage: She puts them on her head.

sp.speaker: Chremylus
sp.p: Those are strange pots indeed! Generally the scum rises to the top of the pots, but here the pots are raised to the top of the old woman.

div.stage: Plutus begins to march solemnly off the stage; the Old Woman follows him.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Let us withdraw without more tarrying, and follow the others, singing as we go.

div.stage: They do so.
